prompt: Which tag creates a hyperlink?
concept_tip: The <a> (anchor) element makes links. Its href attribute holds the destination.
integration_note: Write descriptive link text, not "click here".

prompt: Which tag creates an unordered (bulleted) list?
concept_tip: <ul> wraps bullet items; each item is an <li>. Use <ol> for numbered lists.
integration_note: Use lists for menus and steps; they are easy for screen readers.

prompt: Which element creates a single-line text box in a form?
hints: Its type attribute decides what it looks like.
concept_tip: <input type="text"> is a one-line field. Other types: email, password, number, date.
integration_note: Always give inputs a name so the form data can be read.

prompt: Which attribute stops a form from being submitted while a field is empty?
hints: It is spelled like the English word.
concept_tip: required makes the browser block submit until the field has a value.
integration_note: Browser checks help users, but always validate again on the server.

prompt: What does <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> help with?
options: Making pages display properly on phones
answer: Making pages display properly on phones
hints: Without it, phones zoom out the whole page.
concept_tip: The viewport meta tag tells mobile browsers to use the real screen width.
integration_note: Put it in the <head> of every page.

prompt: Which element should hold the main unique content of a page, once per page?
hints: Its name says what it is.
It should not repeat the header or footer.
concept_tip: <main> marks the central content. Screen readers can jump straight to it.
integration_note: Use only one <main> per page.

prompt: What does the defer attribute on a <script> tag do?
options: Downloads in parallel and runs after the HTML is parsed
Runs the script before anything loads
Loads the script only on phones
answer: Downloads in parallel and runs after the HTML is parsed
hints: Think about not blocking the page.
The script waits for the document.
concept_tip: defer keeps scripts from blocking page rendering and keeps their order.
integration_note: Prefer defer over putting scripts at the end of <body>.

prompt: Which attribute connects a <label> to its form control?
hints: Clicking the label focuses the input.
concept_tip: label for="x" links to the element with id="x". It improves accessibility and click area.
integration_note: Every input should have a label.

prompt: Which property changes the text color?
hints: It is also used for icons using currentColor.
concept_tip: The color property sets the text color.
integration_note: Define colors as variables so the whole site can change at once.

prompt: Which property adds space inside an element, between the content and the border?
hints: Think of padding in a jacket.
concept_tip: padding is inside the border, margin is outside.
integration_note: Use padding to make buttons and cards comfortable to tap.

prompt: Which selector targets the element with id="menu"?
concept_tip: #name selects by id, .name selects by class, name selects by tag.
integration_note: Use classes for styling; ids should be unique.

prompt: Which display value turns an element into a flex container?
concept_tip: display: flex lays children in a row (or column) with easy alignment.
integration_note: Flexbox is perfect for menus and toolbars.

prompt: What does margin: 0 auto; do on a block element with a set width?
hints: auto shares the leftover space left and right.
concept_tip: With a fixed width, auto left and right margins center the block.
integration_note: Combine with max-width to keep layouts readable on large screens.

prompt: Which unit is relative to the root element's font size?
concept_tip: 1rem equals the font size of <html> (usually 16px). It scales with user settings.
integration_note: Use rem for font sizes so users can enlarge text.

prompt: Which rule applies styles only on screens 600px wide or smaller?
hints: max-width means up to that width.
concept_tip: Media queries apply CSS only when a condition is true, which is how responsive design works.
integration_note: Design for mobile first, then add wider rules.

prompt: What does grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); create?
hints: fr means a fraction of free space.
repeat(3, …) repeats the track three times.
concept_tip: 1fr takes an equal share of available width. repeat(3, 1fr) gives three equal columns.
integration_note: Grid is ideal for galleries and dashboards.

prompt: What does typeof "hello" return?
hints: It is not char; JavaScript has no char type.
concept_tip: typeof returns a lowercase string naming the type: string, number, boolean, object, undefined, function.
integration_note: Use typeof to check input before using it.

prompt: Which method adds an item to the end of an array?
hints: Think of pushing onto a stack.
concept_tip: push adds to the end, pop removes the last, unshift adds to the start, shift removes the first.
integration_note: Remember push changes the original array.

prompt: What is the result of 5 + "5" in JavaScript?
concept_tip: If either side of + is a string, JavaScript joins them as text instead of adding.
integration_note: Convert with Number() before doing math on form input.

prompt: Which array method returns a new array containing only the items that pass a test?
hints: It keeps some items and drops others.
concept_tip: filter returns a new array with items for which the callback returns true.
integration_note: Use filter to build search results from a list.

prompt: What does === check?
options: That value and type are both equal
answer: That value and type are both equal
concept_tip: === is strict equality: 5 === '5' is false, while 5 == '5' is true.
integration_note: Prefer === to avoid surprising conversions.

prompt: What does an async function always return?
hints: You can use await on the result.
Even return 5 becomes a resolved value inside it.
concept_tip: async functions wrap their return value in a Promise, so callers use await or .then().
integration_note: Use async/await to make network code read top to bottom.

prompt: What does console.log([1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2)) print?
hints: The original array is not changed.
concept_tip: map returns a new array with the callback applied to each item.
integration_note: Use map to turn data into UI items.

prompt: Inside a regular function called as obj.method(), what does this refer to?
hints: Look at what is left of the dot.
concept_tip: For a method call, this is the object before the dot. Arrow functions inherit this from where they were written.
integration_note: Do not pass methods as callbacks without binding.

prompt: Which line declares a variable age of type number?
hints: The type comes after a colon.
concept_tip: TypeScript adds a : type after the variable name.
integration_note: Types catch mistakes before the code runs.

prompt: What does TypeScript compile to?
hints: It is a superset of a popular web language.
concept_tip: TypeScript is checked at build time and then compiled to plain JavaScript.
integration_note: Run tsc or your bundler to build.

prompt: Which symbol marks a property as optional in an interface?
hints: It goes after the property name.
It means the property may be missing.
concept_tip: name?: string means name can be a string or not be provided at all.
integration_note: Use optional properties for fields users may skip.

prompt: Which keyword can describe the shape of an object and exists only at compile time?
hints: It is erased from the compiled JavaScript.
Classes also describe shapes but exist at runtime.
concept_tip: interface describes the properties an object must have; it produces no JavaScript.
integration_note: Use interfaces for API response shapes.

prompt: What does the type string | number mean?
options: Either a string or a number
A string followed by a number
A function from string to number
Both a string and a number at once
answer: Either a string or a number
hints: This is called a union type.
concept_tip: A union type allows several possible types; narrow it with typeof before use.
integration_note: Unions model values that can be in different forms.

prompt: What return type does a function have if it returns nothing?
hints: It is the opposite of returning a value.
concept_tip: void means the function does not return a useful value.
integration_note: Mark callbacks that return nothing with void.

prompt: Which return type fits a function that always throws an error?
hints: never means no value is ever returned.
concept_tip: never is for functions that never finish normally, like ones that always throw.
integration_note: never also helps make switch statements exhaustive.

prompt: Which type means 'any value, but you must check it before using it'?
hints: any turns checks off; this one keeps them.
Use it for data from outside your program.
concept_tip: unknown is the safe version of any. You must narrow it before using it.
integration_note: Use unknown for JSON from the network.

prompt: Which command installs the packages listed in package.json?
concept_tip: npm install reads package.json and downloads dependencies into node_modules.
integration_note: Run it after cloning any Node project.

prompt: Which built-in module reads and writes files?
hints: The name is short for file system.
concept_tip: fs (file system) can read, write, rename and delete files.
snippet:
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
const text = await readFile('notes.txt', 'utf8');
integration_note: Prefer the promise version (fs/promises).

prompt: What does require('express') do in CommonJS?
hints: Install and load are different steps.
It returns what the module exports.
concept_tip: require loads a module that is already installed, so you must run npm install express first.
snippet:
const express = require('express');
const app = express();
integration_note: Modern code often uses import instead.

prompt: Which file lists a Node project's dependencies and scripts?
concept_tip: package.json stores the name, version, scripts and dependencies.
integration_note: Commit package.json but not node_modules.

prompt: What does process.env.PORT read?
hints: Hosts like Vercel and Render set it.
concept_tip: process.env holds environment variables, used for settings and secrets.
integration_note: Never hard-code passwords; read them from env.

prompt: In Express, what does app.use(express.json()) do?
concept_tip: The JSON middleware converts a JSON request body into req.body.
integration_note: Add it before your routes.

prompt: Why is fs.readFileSync usually avoided inside a request handler?
options: It blocks the event loop while it reads
answer: It blocks the event loop while it reads
hints: Node runs your JavaScript on one thread.
concept_tip: Synchronous calls stop all other requests until they finish. Use async versions in servers.
integration_note: Sync calls are fine in startup scripts.

prompt: What does the Node.js event loop allow?
options: Handling many I/O operations without waiting on each
Using several CPU cores by default
answer: Handling many I/O operations without waiting on each
hints: It is why Node can serve many users at once.
Slow I/O runs in the background.
concept_tip: Node starts I/O work, keeps running other code, and runs callbacks when results arrive.
integration_note: Avoid long CPU loops; they block the loop.

prompt: Which statement reads rows from a table?
concept_tip: SELECT chooses columns to return from a table.
integration_note: SELECT * returns every column; list only what you need.

prompt: Which clause filters rows?
concept_tip: WHERE keeps only rows that match the condition.
integration_note: Combine conditions with AND / OR.

prompt: Which keyword sorts the result?
hints: It goes near the end of the query.
concept_tip: ORDER BY sorts ascending by default; add DESC for descending.
snippet:
SELECT name, xp FROM students
ORDER BY xp DESC;
integration_note: Pair with LIMIT for top-N lists.

prompt: Which function counts rows?
concept_tip: COUNT(*) returns the number of rows in the group or table.
snippet:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students
WHERE gender = 'female';
integration_note: Use COUNT for dashboards.

prompt: Which join returns only rows that match in both tables?
hints: LEFT keeps all rows from the first table.
It uses ON to match keys.
concept_tip: INNER JOIN keeps only matching pairs; LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table.
integration_note: Always give the join an ON condition.

prompt: Which clause filters groups after GROUP BY?
concept_tip: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters the grouped results.
snippet:
SELECT batch_year, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM students
GROUP BY batch_year
HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;
integration_note: Use HAVING with aggregate conditions.

prompt: What does a PRIMARY KEY guarantee?
options: Each row has a unique, non-null identifier
answer: Each row has a unique, non-null identifier
concept_tip: A primary key uniquely identifies each row and cannot be NULL.
integration_note: Other tables reference it with a FOREIGN KEY.

prompt: Why use parameterized queries ($1, ?) instead of joining strings?
options: It makes every query twice as fast
It removes the need for indexes
hints: User input becomes data, not code.
concept_tip: Parameters are sent separately from the SQL text, so input cannot change the query.
integration_note: Use parameters in every query that includes user input.

prompt: What is JSX?
hints: A compiler turns it into JavaScript.
concept_tip: JSX lets you describe UI with tags in JavaScript. React turns it into function calls.
integration_note: Components must return a single parent element.

prompt: Which hook stores state in a function component?
hints: It returns a value and a setter.
Its name contains the word state.
concept_tip: useState returns the current value and a function to update it.
integration_note: Changing state re-renders the component.

prompt: How do you pass data from a parent component to a child?
hints: They are read-only in the child.
concept_tip: Props are inputs to a component, passed as attributes.
integration_note: Props flow down, never up.

prompt: Which hook runs code after render, such as fetching data?
hints: The second argument is a dependency array.
concept_tip: useEffect runs after React updates the screen, ideal for data fetching and subscriptions.
integration_note: Always list the values the effect uses in the array.

prompt: Why does a list rendered with .map() need a key prop?
options: It helps React track which items changed
answer: It helps React track which items changed
hints: Keys must be unique among siblings.
Index keys can cause bugs when reordering.
concept_tip: Keys let React match old and new items so it updates the right DOM nodes.
integration_note: Use a stable id, not the array index.

prompt: What happens when you call setCount(count + 1)?
options: React re-renders with the new value
count changes immediately in the same function
answer: React re-renders with the new value
hints: The next render sees the new value.
concept_tip: Setting state asks React to re-render; the new value appears in the next render.
integration_note: Use setCount(c => c + 1) when you rely on the previous value.

prompt: What does an empty dependency array, useEffect(fn, []), mean?
options: Run once after the first render
answer: Run once after the first render
hints: Nothing in the array can change.
Commonly used for initial data loading.
concept_tip: With [] the effect has no dependencies, so it runs after the first render only.
integration_note: Leaving out the array runs the effect on every render.

prompt: Why should state never be changed directly (like items.push(x))?
options: React may not notice the change and not re-render
answer: React may not notice the change and not re-render
hints: React compares old and new references.
concept_tip: React detects changes when you give it a new value. Mutating the old one hides the change.
integration_note: Copy arrays and objects before changing them.

prompt: What does an IP address identify?
hints: Your phone gets one when it joins Wi-Fi.
concept_tip: An IP address locates a device on a network so data knows where to go.
integration_note: Private ranges like 192.168.x.x work only inside your network.

prompt: Which protocol loads web pages securely?
hints: Look for the padlock in the browser.
concept_tip: HTTPS is HTTP wrapped in TLS encryption.
integration_note: Use HTTPS for every site, especially login pages.

prompt: What is the default port for HTTP?
concept_tip: HTTP uses port 80 by default.
integration_note: Open only the ports you need on a server.

prompt: What is the default port for HTTPS?
concept_tip: HTTPS uses port 443 by default.
integration_note: Your VPS needs ports 80 and 443 open.

prompt: Which device forwards packets between different networks?
hints: It connects your home to the internet.
concept_tip: A router chooses where to send packets between networks.
integration_note: Your default gateway is your router.

prompt: What does DHCP do?
options: Automatically assigns IP addresses to devices
answer: Automatically assigns IP addresses to devices
hints: It is why you rarely type an IP on Wi-Fi.
concept_tip: DHCP hands out IP addresses, gateways and DNS servers when a device joins.
integration_note: Static addresses are used for servers.

prompt: Which protocol is connection-oriented and guarantees ordered delivery?
hints: UDP skips these checks for speed.
concept_tip: TCP sets up a connection, numbers packets and resends lost ones. UDP is faster but unreliable.
snippet:
TCP: web, email, SSH
UDP: video calls, DNS, games
integration_note: Choose UDP only when speed matters more than perfect delivery.

prompt: What does a /24 subnet mask (255.255.255.0) mean?
options: The first 24 bits identify the network
answer: The first 24 bits identify the network
concept_tip: /24 means 24 network bits and 8 host bits, so 256 addresses (254 usable).
integration_note: Subnets keep networks organised and secure.

prompt: Which command lists the files in a directory?
concept_tip: ls lists files. Add -l for details and -a for hidden files.
integration_note: Combine flags like -la.

prompt: Which command prints the current directory?
concept_tip: pwd shows the full path of where you are.
integration_note: Use it when you get lost in the terminal.

prompt: Which command creates a new directory?
concept_tip: mkdir creates folders; -p creates parent folders too.
integration_note: Use -p to avoid errors if it already exists.

prompt: Which command changes file permissions?
concept_tip: chmod sets who can read, write or execute a file.
integration_note: Make scripts executable before running them.

prompt: What does the pipe | do in cat log.txt | grep error?
options: Sends one command's output into the next
answer: Sends one command's output into the next
hints: The output of cat becomes the input of grep.
concept_tip: A pipe connects the output of one command to the input of another.
integration_note: Pipes let you build powerful one-liners.

prompt: Which command searches for text inside files?
concept_tip: grep prints lines that match a pattern; -r searches folders and -i ignores case.
integration_note: Great for hunting secrets accidentally left in code.

prompt: What does chmod 755 script.sh give the owner?
hints: The first digit is for the owner.
concept_tip: Digits are owner, group, others. 7 = read+write+execute, 5 = read+execute.
integration_note: Never use 777 on a real server.

prompt: What does > do in echo hi > file.txt?
concept_tip: > sends output to a file and replaces its contents. >> appends.
snippet:
$ echo hi > file.txt
$ echo again >> file.txt
integration_note: Double-check before using > on important files.

prompt: Which Python library is commonly used to send HTTP requests?
hints: Its name is a plural noun.
concept_tip: requests makes HTTP calls simple: get, post, headers, JSON.
integration_note: Always set a timeout on requests.

prompt: Which function reads text typed by the user?
concept_tip: input() waits for the user to type and returns what they typed as text.
integration_note: Treat user input as untrusted.

prompt: Which module provides low-level network sockets?
hints: Used to build clients and servers by hand.
Port scanners are built on it.
concept_tip: The socket module connects to IP addresses and ports directly.
snippet:
import socket
s = socket.socket()
s.settimeout(1)
print(s.connect_ex(('127.0.0.1', 80)))
integration_note: Only scan systems you own or have permission to test.

prompt: Which built-in module computes SHA-256 hashes?
hints: It also supports MD5 and SHA-1.
concept_tip: hashlib creates fixed-size fingerprints of data.
integration_note: Use hashes to verify file integrity.

prompt: Which module should generate secure random tokens?
hints: It is designed for passwords and tokens.
concept_tip: secrets uses the operating system's secure random generator.
integration_note: Use it for invite codes and reset links.

prompt: What does the pattern 'with open(path) as f:' guarantee?
options: The file is created in memory
hints: It cleans up when the block ends.
concept_tip: A with block closes the file for you, even if an exception occurs.
integration_note: Prevents leaked file handles.

prompt: Why is subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True) with user input dangerous?
hints: Input like ; rm -rf can be added.
concept_tip: With shell=True, text is passed to the shell, so attackers can add extra commands.
snippet:
# unsafe
subprocess.run(f'ping {host}', shell=True)
# safer
subprocess.run(['ping', '-c', '1', host])
integration_note: Pass arguments as a list and validate input.

prompt: Which approach stores passwords safely?
options: Hash with a slow salted algorithm like bcrypt or argon2
answer: Hash with a slow salted algorithm like bcrypt or argon2
hints: Plain text and base64 can be read back.
concept_tip: bcrypt and argon2 add a salt and are deliberately slow, which protects against brute force.
snippet:
import bcrypt
hashed = bcrypt.hashpw(b'pw123', bcrypt.gensalt())
print(bcrypt.checkpw(b'pw123', hashed))
integration_note: Never store or log real passwords.

prompt: What does XSS stand for?
hints: It involves injecting script into pages.
The X replaces the word Cross.
concept_tip: XSS lets attackers run their JavaScript in other users' browsers through unsafe input.
integration_note: Use textContent instead of innerHTML for user data.

prompt: Which attack inserts malicious SQL into a query?
concept_tip: SQL injection tricks the database into running attacker-written commands.
snippet:
-- input: ' OR '1'='1
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '' OR '1'='1';
integration_note: Never build SQL from raw user input.

prompt: What does HTTPS add over HTTP?
hints: It protects data on the way.
concept_tip: HTTPS encrypts data between browser and server, so others on the network cannot read it.
snippet:
https://  → encrypted
http://   → readable by anyone on the path
integration_note: Redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS.

prompt: What is CSRF?
options: Tricking a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request
Stealing a password with a keylogger
answer: Tricking a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request
hints: A hidden form on another site can trigger it.
concept_tip: CSRF abuses the fact that browsers attach cookies to requests. Defend with SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens.
integration_note: Require a token for state-changing requests.

prompt: Which cookie flag stops JavaScript from reading the cookie?
hints: It protects against stolen sessions via XSS.
concept_tip: HttpOnly cookies are sent to the server but hidden from document.cookie.
integration_note: Set HttpOnly on all session cookies.

prompt: What is the best defence against XSS when showing user text?
options: Escape or encode it before output
answer: Escape or encode it before output
hints: Frameworks like React do this by default.
concept_tip: Output encoding turns special characters into safe text so the browser does not run them.
integration_note: Never insert raw user input into HTML.

prompt: What does the Content-Security-Policy header do?
options: Limits which sources a page may load scripts and resources from
answer: Limits which sources a page may load scripts and resources from
hints: It is an extra layer against XSS.
The server sends it as a header.
concept_tip: CSP tells the browser which scripts, images and frames are allowed.
integration_note: Start strict and loosen only when needed.

prompt: Why should you not show detailed error messages (stack traces) to users?
options: They can reveal internal details to attackers
answer: They can reveal internal details to attackers
hints: Paths, versions and queries help attackers.
Log details on the server instead.
concept_tip: Detailed errors leak file paths, libraries and database information. Show a simple message and log the rest.
integration_note: Return generic errors to the client.

prompt: Which kind of encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt?
hints: Both sides share one secret key.
concept_tip: Symmetric encryption is fast and uses one shared key. The challenge is sharing the key safely.
snippet:
# one key does both jobs
ciphertext = encrypt(key, message)
message = decrypt(key, ciphertext)
integration_note: Used for encrypting files and traffic once keys are agreed.

prompt: Which operation is one-way, so you cannot get the original back?
hints: Encryption can be decrypted with a key.
concept_tip: A hash turns data into a fixed-size fingerprint that cannot be reversed.
integration_note: Verify downloads by comparing hashes.

prompt: Which of these is a hash function?
concept_tip: SHA-256 is a widely used cryptographic hash. AES and RSA are encryption algorithms.
integration_note: Use SHA-256 or better for integrity checks.

prompt: In public-key cryptography, which key do you share with others?
hints: The other one must stay secret.
Anyone can use it to send you data.
concept_tip: Share your public key freely; keep the private key secret.
snippet:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
# share id_ed25519.pub, never id_ed25519
integration_note: If a private key leaks, replace the pair.

prompt: Which algorithm is a widely used symmetric cipher?
concept_tip: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is the standard symmetric cipher.
snippet:
from cryptography.fernet import Fernet
key = Fernet.generate_key()
token = Fernet(key).encrypt(b'secret')
integration_note: Use well-tested libraries; never invent your own crypto.

prompt: What is a salt in password hashing?
options: Random data added to each password before hashing
A secret key kept in the browser
answer: Random data added to each password before hashing
hints: Two identical passwords get different hashes.
concept_tip: A unique salt per password stops attackers from using rainbow tables.
integration_note: Libraries like bcrypt add salts automatically.

prompt: Why is MD5 not recommended for passwords?
options: It is fast and has known collisions
answer: It is fast and has known collisions
hints: Different inputs can share a hash.
concept_tip: MD5 is broken for security use and attackers can test billions of guesses per second.
snippet:
# avoid
hashlib.md5(password).hexdigest()
# prefer bcrypt or argon2
integration_note: Use slow password hashes, not general-purpose ones.

prompt: What does a digital signature prove?
options: Who created a message and that it was not changed
answer: Who created a message and that it was not changed
hints: It uses the sender's private key.
Anyone can check it with the public key.
concept_tip: A signature gives authenticity and integrity, not secrecy.
snippet:
# sign with private key
sig = private_key.sign(data)
# verify with public key
public_key.verify(sig, data)
integration_note: Git commits and software updates are often signed.

prompt: What does len("python") return?
concept_tip: len returns the number of characters in a string or items in a list.
integration_note: Check len(x) > 0 before using values.

prompt: Which symbol starts a comment in Python?
hints: Everything after it on the line is ignored.
concept_tip: A # starts a comment that runs to the end of the line.
integration_note: Write comments that explain why, not what.

prompt: What type is {'a': 1}?
concept_tip: A dictionary maps keys to values.
integration_note: Use dicts for records.

prompt: What does [x*x for x in range(4)] produce?
concept_tip: A list comprehension builds a list from a loop in one line.
integration_note: Great for transforming data.

prompt: What does range(3) generate?
concept_tip: range(3) produces 0, 1 and 2.
integration_note: Use range for counting loops.

prompt: Which keywords handle errors in Python?
hints: Risky code goes in the first block.
The second block handles the error.
concept_tip: try runs code that might fail; except handles the failure.
integration_note: Catch specific errors, not everything.

prompt: What does a Python decorator do?
options: Wraps a function to add behavior
answer: Wraps a function to add behavior
hints: It is written with @ above a function.
concept_tip: A decorator takes a function and returns an improved version.
integration_note: Frameworks use decorators for routes.

prompt: How does a list differ from a tuple?
options: A list is mutable, a tuple is not
A list is faster to read
answer: A list is mutable, a tuple is not
hints: Can you change items after creating it?
concept_tip: Lists can be changed after creation; tuples cannot.
integration_note: Use tuples for fixed data like coordinates.

prompt: Which library is used for fast numerical arrays?
hints: Its name stands for numerical Python.
Many data libraries build on it.
concept_tip: NumPy provides n-dimensional arrays and fast math on them.
snippet:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
print(a * 2)
integration_note: Vectorised operations are much faster than loops.

prompt: Which library provides the DataFrame?
hints: A table with rows and columns.
concept_tip: A pandas DataFrame is a table of data with labeled columns.
snippet:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('students.csv')
integration_note: Use pandas to clean and analyse club data.

prompt: How is NumPy normally imported?
hints: Everyone uses the same short alias.
concept_tip: The convention is import numpy as np.
integration_note: Following conventions helps others read your code.

prompt: What does df.head() show?
hints: A quick peek at the data.
concept_tip: head() shows the first rows (5 by default).
integration_note: Always inspect data before analysing.

prompt: What is the shape of np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])?
concept_tip: This array has 2 rows and 3 columns.
integration_note: Check shapes when debugging errors.

prompt: Which method drops rows with missing values?
concept_tip: dropna removes rows (or columns) that contain NaN.
integration_note: Decide whether to drop or fill missing data.

prompt: What does np.mean(a, axis=0) compute for a 2D array?
concept_tip: axis=0 collapses rows, giving one result per column.
integration_note: Axis confusion is a common bug.

prompt: What does df.groupby('team')['score'].mean() return?
options: The average score for each team
answer: The average score for each team
concept_tip: groupby splits data by a column; then you apply a summary like mean.
integration_note: Use groupby for summaries by category.

prompt: Which type of learning uses labeled examples?
hints: Each example has the right answer attached.
concept_tip: In supervised learning, the model learns from inputs paired with correct outputs.
integration_note: Most business ML problems are supervised.

prompt: Predicting a house price is which kind of task?
concept_tip: Regression predicts a continuous number.
snippet:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
model = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
integration_note: Price, temperature and score are regression targets.

prompt: Predicting whether an email is spam or not is which task?
hints: The answer is one of a few categories.
concept_tip: Classification predicts a category label.
snippet:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
model = LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)
integration_note: Yes/no problems are classification.

prompt: Why do we split data into training and test sets?
options: To check performance on unseen data
answer: To check performance on unseen data
hints: The model should not be graded on what it already saw.
concept_tip: A test set simulates new data, showing whether the model generalises.
snippet:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2)
integration_note: Never tune a model on the test set.

prompt: What is overfitting?
options: The model memorises training data and fails on new data
The data is too small to load
answer: The model memorises training data and fails on new data
hints: High training score, low test score.
concept_tip: An overfit model fits the training data too closely and performs poorly on new data.
integration_note: Use more data, simpler models or regularisation.

prompt: Which library offers easy classic ML models like LogisticRegression?
concept_tip: scikit-learn provides ready-made models, preprocessing and evaluation tools.
snippet:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
model = RandomForestClassifier().fit(X_tr, y_tr)
integration_note: Start with scikit-learn before deep learning.

prompt: What does accuracy measure?
options: The share of predictions that are correct
answer: The share of predictions that are correct
hints: Correct predictions divided by all predictions.
It can mislead with unbalanced data.
concept_tip: accuracy = correct predictions / total predictions.
snippet:
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score
print(accuracy_score(y_te, model.predict(X_te)))
integration_note: With rare events, also check precision and recall.

prompt: What does k-means do?
concept_tip: k-means assigns each point to the nearest of k cluster centres.
snippet:
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
labels = KMeans(n_clusters=3).fit_predict(X)
integration_note: Use clustering to discover groups without labels.

prompt: What is a neural network made of?
concept_tip: A neural network stacks layers of simple units called neurons.
snippet:
import torch.nn as nn
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4, 8), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(8, 1))
integration_note: Depth means many layers.

prompt: Which are popular deep learning frameworks?
concept_tip: PyTorch and TensorFlow build and train neural networks.
integration_note: Pick one and learn it well.

prompt: What is an epoch?
options: One full pass over the training data
answer: One full pass over the training data
concept_tip: An epoch is a complete cycle through the training set.
integration_note: Watch the loss across epochs.

prompt: What does a loss function measure?
options: How wrong the model's predictions are
answer: How wrong the model's predictions are
hints: Training tries to make it small.
concept_tip: The loss gives a single number for the model's error.
integration_note: Pick a loss that fits the task.

prompt: What does gradient descent do?
options: Adjusts weights to reduce the loss
answer: Adjusts weights to reduce the loss
hints: It walks downhill on the error.
concept_tip: Gradient descent updates the weights a little at a time in the direction that lowers the loss.
integration_note: Optimisers like Adam are smarter versions.

prompt: Which network type is commonly used for images?
concept_tip: CNNs use filters that slide across an image to detect patterns.
integration_note: Use pretrained CNNs for small datasets.

prompt: What does dropout do during training?
options: Randomly turns off neurons to reduce overfitting
answer: Randomly turns off neurons to reduce overfitting
hints: The network cannot rely on one neuron.
It is switched off at test time.
concept_tip: Dropout forces the network to learn robust features by randomly ignoring neurons.
integration_note: Call model.eval() when predicting.

prompt: What does the learning rate control?
options: The size of each weight update step
answer: The size of each weight update step
hints: Too big overshoots, too small is slow.
concept_tip: A larger learning rate takes bigger steps; too large can make training unstable.
integration_note: Tune it first when training misbehaves.
